label: A
public_title: Computer use at school and 15-year-olds' reading scores
card:
**What was studied.** How often 15-year-olds use computers at school, and how that use relates to their performance on an international assessment of reading, mathematics, and science. The data come from the 2012 round of a large international survey in which students in dozens of countries sit the same tests and answer questionnaires about computer access and use. In the participating wealthy countries, 96% of students reported a computer at home and 72% reported using one at school.

**How.** A secondary analysis of cross-sectional survey data. The report builds an index of how frequently students do a range of things on computers at school (browsing, email, chatting, drill and practice) and plots average test performance against that index, after adjusting for the socioeconomic status of students and schools. It also compares countries: how much each invested in school technology and how its scores changed over time.

**What was found.** The relationship between school computer use and reading performance is, in the report's words, "graphically illustrated by a hill shape." Students who used computers slightly less than the average did best. Students who used them rarely did somewhat worse, and students who used them much more than average did a lot worse, even after adjustment. At the country level, "resources invested in ICT for education are not linked to improved student achievement in reading, mathematics or science," and countries that invested less improved faster. The report's foreword summarizes the classroom evidence as "mixed at best."

**Limitations the authors state.** The report is unusually direct: with "non-experimental, cross-sectional data such as those gathered through [this assessment], even sophisticated statistical techniques cannot isolate the cause-and-effect relationship." The analyses cannot account for prior achievement. Schools may give computers to struggling students, or heavy users may differ from light users "in terms of their aptitude, behaviour and disposition towards learning and school."

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The index mixes browsing, chatting, and email with instructional software. A hill-shaped curve for that index says little about any particular learning tool. The data are from 2012.

**Who produced it and why.** An intergovernmental economic organization produced the report through its secretariat, steered by a board of participating governments. It is not peer reviewed in the journal sense but is the organization's flagship education publication. No external sponsor is named and no conflicts are declared.

label: B
public_title: Online math practice and growth on an interim assessment
card:
**What was studied.** A free online mathematics practice platform, built by a nonprofit provider in partnership with the maker of a widely used computer-adaptive interim assessment. The platform assigns practice based on each student's fall assessment results. The data cover 181,359 students in grades 3 to 8 from 99 school districts and 649 schools in the United States during the 2020–21 school year, a year disrupted by the pandemic. About half the students attended schools where most students qualified for free or reduced-price lunch.

**How.** This was not an experiment. Students were sorted into four groups by how much they used the platform: none, under 15 minutes a week, 15 to 29 minutes, and 30 or more minutes. The provider's recommended dose is 30 minutes a week, roughly one class period. The authors compared fall-to-spring growth across the usage groups, adjusting for fall scores, demographics, and school, district, and teacher effects. They also compared math growth with reading growth for the same students, reasoning that an unmeasured factor affecting both subjects would show up in reading, which the platform does not teach.

**What was found.** Students who used the platform 30 or more minutes a week grew 0.26 standard deviations more in math than similar students who used it less than 15 minutes a week (95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.31). The association was positive across gender, racial and ethnic groups, and school poverty levels, and smaller in districts with many English learners. Only 5% of students reached the recommended dose; 41% never used the platform.

**Limitations the authors state.** In their words, "this was still an observational study and does not provide the same quality of causal evidence as a randomized control trial." The math-versus-reading comparison assumes unmeasured factors affect both subjects equally, which they call unknown. Heavier users also showed higher reading growth, which the authors say "suggests possible unobserved confounding." The year was pandemic-disrupted.

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The students who chose to use the platform for 30 minutes a week, in a year when most students did not, may differ in motivation, teacher support, or home circumstances in ways that no set of controls removes. The 5% figure is both a finding about implementation and a warning about who is in the comparison.

**Who produced it and why.** The report was written by three researchers employed by the organization that makes the platform. It was reviewed by an external advisory board but not peer reviewed. The organization's sales page for districts cites the finding as evidence that the platform "accelerates learning." No funding statement appears in the report.

label: C
kind: Rigorous but dated national randomized trial
public_title: A national experiment on reading and math software

figure.alt: Bar chart of effect sizes near zero for four first-grade reading outcomes; none significantly different from zero.
figure.caption: Effects of first-grade reading products on a standardized reading test, in effect-size units. Reproduced from the source report, which is in the public domain.

card:
**What was studied.** Whether commercial reading and mathematics software raised test scores. Federal legislation in 2001 required the national education department to study the effectiveness of educational technology using "scientifically based research methods and control groups." Sixteen products were chosen from public submissions and expert review, grouped into first-grade reading, fourth-grade reading, sixth-grade mathematics, and algebra. The study ran in the 2004–05 school year.

**How.** A randomized controlled trial. Within each school, volunteering teachers were randomly assigned to use a study product or not. Control teachers could keep using whatever other technology was already in their classrooms. Thirty-three districts, 132 schools, and 439 teachers took part; 9,424 students were in the analysis sample. Outcomes were nationally normed standardized tests in reading and mathematics and a standard algebra end-of-course test. Effects were estimated with models that account for students nested in classrooms and schools.

**What was found.** "Test scores in treatment classrooms that were randomly assigned to use products did not differ from test scores in control classrooms by statistically significant margins." In first grade, effect sizes ranged from −0.01 to 0.06 standard deviations, equivalent to zero to two percentile points, none significant. The pattern held in each grade and subject. Effects of reading products were larger in first-grade classrooms with fewer students per teacher and in fourth-grade classrooms that used the product more.

**Limitations the authors state.** Companies volunteered their products, so the products "were not a representative sampling" of software in use, and the department acknowledged that choosing promising products could tilt the study toward finding effects. Vendors suggested many participating districts, trained the teachers, and provided technical support. Control teachers also used technology, about a fifth as much.

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The products are two decades old. The study says what software of that era did in one year of use; it does not speak to adaptive platforms, tutoring software, or AI tools, and anyone citing it today must argue for why the result transfers.

**Who produced it and why.** Two independent contract research firms conducted the study under contract to the federal education department, which reported it to the national legislature. Vendors participated on the understanding that results would be reported only for groups of products, not by name. The report is in the public domain.

label: D
public_title: How many teachers and students use AI for schoolwork
card:
**What was studied.** How widely students and teachers in U.S. public schools use artificial intelligence tools, how often, and whether schools provide guidance. The report does not estimate any effect on learning. It describes use, drawing on eight nationally representative survey panels of students, parents, teachers, principals, and district leaders fielded between October 2024 and June 2025, plus ten interviews with district leaders.

**How.** Descriptive, weighted tabulations of survey responses. The largest sample is 8,601 English language arts, mathematics, and science teachers surveyed in spring 2025 and asked how frequently they had used AI tools for instructional planning or teaching that school year. Students were 1,261 middle and high schoolers surveyed in early 2025. Weights make the results nationally representative of each population.

**What was found.** In 2025, 54% of middle and high school students said they used AI for schoolwork to some extent, and 21% at least weekly; use rose from 41% in middle school to 61% in high school. Among teachers, 53% reported using AI for planning or teaching, about 13% weekly; 42% of elementary teachers, 64% of middle school teachers, and 69% of high school teachers. A year earlier the teacher figure was 25%. Thirty-five percent of district leaders said they had trained students on AI, and over 80% of students said no teacher had explicitly taught them how to use it for schoolwork. Forty-five percent of principals reported a school or district AI policy.

**Limitations the authors state.** The findings are self-reports of use, not measures of what students or teachers did with the tools or what they learned. The question asked about any AI tool, from chatbots to features built into existing software.

**A limitation the authors do not state.** None of these numbers says whether AI use helps or harms achievement. The study's value is in telling us how fast a technology is spreading ahead of guidance, which is a different question from the one the other studies ask. The teacher sample was limited to three subjects.

**Who produced it and why.** A nonprofit policy research organization produced the report with its own funds and gifts from supporters, in partnership with two university research centers. The report is not peer reviewed. It does not sell or evaluate any product.

label: E
public_title: Home computer vouchers for low-income families
card:
**What was studied.** A national government program in an Eastern European country gave low-income families a voucher worth about 200 euros toward a home computer. In 2008, 52,212 households applied and met the income threshold; the budget covered 35,484 vouchers, so applicants were ranked by family income per household member and vouchers went to those below a cutoff. The question was whether having a computer at home changed children's school performance and skills.

**How.** A regression discontinuity design. Families just below the income cutoff received vouchers; families just above did not. Because the two groups are nearly identical in income, comparing them isolates the effect of the voucher. Researchers surveyed 3,354 families in 2009, about 52% of those contacted, covering roughly 5,900 children aged 7 to 19. Outcomes were school grades in mathematics, the national language, and English, a test of computer skills, a nonverbal reasoning test, and parent and child reports on how the computer was used.

**What was found.** Winning a voucher raised the probability of owning a computer by more than 50 percentage points and increased children's computer use by three to four hours a week. Children in voucher-winning households had lower grades in all three subjects, with most estimates near one third of a standard deviation. They scored higher on the computer-skills test and on the reasoning test, also by about one third of a standard deviation. Few computers had educational software; most had games. Children who won a voucher were 14 percentage points more likely to play computer games daily and reported less time on homework. Where parents had rules about homework, the negative effect on grades was about half as large.

**Limitations the authors state.** The design identifies the effect for families near the income cutoff, not for all families. The response rate was 52%. The evidence on parental rules is, in the authors' words, "merely suggestive since such rules are not randomly assigned."

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The study is from 2008 and 2009, before smartphones were widespread and before most learning software existed. Whether a home computer today would be used the same way is a separate question.

**Who produced it and why.** Two university economists in the United States conducted the study, with funding from private research foundations and university research centers. The paper was published in a peer-reviewed economics journal. Neither author had a relationship with a technology vendor that the paper discloses.

label: F
kind: Impact evaluation, large multi-site randomized trial
public_title: High-dosage tutoring at scale after the pandemic
card:
**What was studied.** High-dosage tutoring, meaning small-group tutoring several times a week during the school day, often delivered with the support of software and in some sites by remote tutors. The study asked whether tutoring produces learning gains when districts run it at scale, and whether a lower-cost version works as well. Data cover 2023–24 across eight state, district, and charter partners in the United States, grades K to 12, in mathematics and reading.

**How.** A randomized controlled trial. 17,330 students were randomly assigned to standard high-dosage tutoring (about $2,000 per student), a "sustainable" lower-cost version (about $1,200 per student, with larger groups or more technology), or business as usual. The analytic sample was 16,435 students. Outcomes were standardized test scores. The report gives both the effect of being assigned to tutoring and the effect for students who actually received it.

**What was found.** Pooled effects of being assigned to tutoring were 0.046 standard deviations for the standard version and 0.065 for the lower-cost version, about one to two months of additional learning. Effects for students who received tutoring were 0.055 and 0.085. Across sites, the standard version's effects ranged from 0.008 to 0.13 standard deviations. Students received far less tutoring than planned: 631 to 2,287 minutes a year, against 2,030 to 4,940 in the earlier small studies that motivated the program. The authors conclude, "Lower cost models ($1200 per student) are just as effective as higher cost models ($2000 per student)."

**Limitations the authors state.** All findings are labeled preliminary. Comparison students were also receiving pandemic-recovery services funded by federal relief money, which the authors say may mask the true effect of tutoring. Dosage "falls far short of what would be needed to fully realize the promise of high dosage tutoring."

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The pooled estimate averages over sites whose programs, tutors, and software differed. A district adopting one of these models is adopting one site's program, not the average.

**Who produced it and why.** A university research lab and a nonprofit evaluation firm produced the interim report, with funding from a list of private foundations and individual donors, several of whom also fund tutoring programs. The report has not been peer reviewed. Neither organization sells tutoring.

label: G
kind: Impact evaluation, randomized trial of an AI tool
public_title: Six weeks of after-school tutoring with a generative AI chatbot

figure.alt: Distributions of combined assessment scores for treatment and control students; the treatment distribution sits to the right.
figure.caption: Distribution of combined assessment scores by treatment condition. Reproduced from the source report under its open license; attribution given at reveal.

card:
**What was studied.** An after-school program in which first-year senior secondary students in a West African city used a general-purpose generative AI chatbot, powered by a large commercial language model, to practice English. Students met twice a week for six weeks in school computer labs, twelve 90-minute sessions in all, working in pairs on one computer with a teacher present. The question was whether the program improved English achievement.

**How.** A randomized controlled trial. Nine public schools with computer labs were selected. Of eligible students, 52% expressed interest; from that pool, 657 were randomly assigned to the program and 671 to a control group that received nothing. The outcome was an assessment covering English topics aligned with the national curriculum, knowledge of artificial intelligence, and digital skills, plus the school's regular end-of-term English exam.

**What was found.** Students in the program scored 0.31 standard deviations higher on the combined assessment (standard error 0.068) and 0.23 standard deviations higher on the English portion. The effect on the school's own term exam was 0.21 standard deviations. Effects were largest for girls and for students with higher starting scores. The authors translate the gain into "1.5 to 2 years of 'business-as-usual' schooling."

**Limitations the authors state.** Attrition was high and uneven: 422 of 657 treated students and 337 of 671 control students completed the final assessment. The authors report bounds that remain positive under conservative assumptions about who dropped out. Participants were volunteers from schools that already had computer labs, and the authors call for longer programs and rural schools before generalizing.

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The program bundled a chatbot with twelve extra sessions of supervised English practice. The design cannot separate the chatbot from the added time with a teacher present. The "years of schooling" translation also depends on a benchmark for how much students in this setting learn per year, which the report takes from other sources.

**Who produced it and why.** Six researchers at an international development bank wrote the working paper, with financial support from a private foundation. The chatbot was a free commercial product; the paper describes the product but reports no funding, co-design, or other role for its maker. The paper is a working paper, not peer reviewed.

label: H
kind: Impact evaluation, randomized trial of an AI tool
public_title: Generative AI during math practice in high school
card:
**What was studied.** Whether giving high school students access to a large language model while they practice mathematics helps or hurts what they learn. The study took place in one large high school in Turkey during fall 2023, in about fifty 9th, 10th, and 11th grade classes with nearly 1,000 students, over four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the semester's math curriculum.

**How.** A randomized controlled trial with classrooms assigned to one of three conditions. In one, students practiced with a chat interface built on a frontier commercial model, similar to the public chatbot. In a second, students used the same model behind prompts written to act as a tutor, giving hints without full solutions. The control condition practiced with notes and the textbook. Each session had a review lecture, a practice period, and then a closed-book exam on similar problems with no AI access. The design and analysis were preregistered.

**What was found.** During practice, students with the plain chatbot did 48% better than control, and students with the tutor version did 127% better. On the unassisted exam, students who had used the plain chatbot scored 17% worse than control; the difference was statistically significant. Students who had used the tutor version scored the same as control. The plain chatbot gave a wrong final answer with a logical error 42% of the time and an arithmetic error 8% of the time on the practice problems. The authors conclude students "attempt to use [the chatbot] as a 'crutch' during practice problem sessions, and when successful, perform worse on their own."

**Limitations the authors state.** One school, one semester, four sessions. Students' own assessments of how much they learned were "overly optimistic."

What was studied. Whether giving high school students access to a large language model while they practice mathematics helps or hurts what they learn. The study took place in one large high school in Turkey during fall 2023, in about fifty 9th, 10th, and 11th grade classes with nearly 1,000 students, over four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the semester’s math curriculum.

How. A randomized controlled trial with classrooms assigned to one of three conditions. In one, students practiced with a chat interface built on a frontier commercial model, similar to the public chatbot. In a second, students used the same model behind prompts written to act as a tutor, giving hints without full solutions. The control condition practiced with notes and the textbook. Each session had a review lecture, a practice period, and then a closed-book exam on similar problems with no AI access. The design and analysis were preregistered.

What was found. During practice, students with the plain chatbot did 48% better than control, and students with the tutor version did 127% better. On the unassisted exam, students who had used the plain chatbot scored 17% worse than control; the difference was statistically significant. Students who had used the tutor version scored the same as control. The plain chatbot gave a wrong final answer with a logical error 42% of the time and an arithmetic error 8% of the time on the practice problems. The authors conclude students “attempt to use [the chatbot] as a ‘crutch’ during practice problem sessions, and when successful, perform worse on their own.”

label: I
kind: Longitudinal correlational study of screen time
public_title: Screen time and developmental screening in early childhood
card:
**What was studied.** Whether the amount of time young children spend in front of screens predicts their performance on a developmental screening test, and whether the relationship runs the other way. The study followed 2,441 mother–child pairs from a Canadian city, with data collected when children were 24, 36, and 60 months old, between 2011 and 2016.

**How.** A longitudinal cohort study. Mothers reported their child's weekly screen time and completed a standard developmental screening questionnaire covering communication, motor skills, problem solving, and personal-social development at each age. The analysis used a cross-lagged panel model, which tests whether screen time at one age predicts development at the next age, and whether development predicts later screen time, while separating stable differences between children from changes within a child over time.

**What was found.** Average screen time was 17 hours a week at 24 months, 25 hours at 36 months, and 11 hours at 60 months. Higher screen time at 24 months predicted lower developmental scores at 36 months (standardized coefficient −0.06; 95% CI −0.10 to −0.01), and higher screen time at 36 months predicted lower scores at 60 months (−0.08; 95% CI −0.13 to −0.02). Lower development did not predict later screen time. The authors write that "the results of this study support the directional association between screen time and child development."

**Limitations the authors state.** Both screen time and development were reported by mothers. The screening questionnaire is a screening tool, not a diagnostic test. The paper's abstract was corrected after publication because two coefficients had been transposed; the correction did not change the conclusion.

**A limitation the authors do not state.** The study measured total screen time, mostly television and video, in children aged two to five. It did not measure instructional software or any use in school. Coefficients of −0.06 to −0.08 are small, and the study cannot say what else in a household changes when a two-year-old watches 17 hours a week.

**Who produced it and why.** University psychologists and pediatric researchers in Canada conducted the study with funding from a provincial health research agency, a children's hospital foundation, and a national research chairs program. The paper was peer reviewed in a pediatrics journal. The funders had no role in the analysis. No author reported a relationship with a technology company.

label: N
public_title: News coverage: "Computers 'do not improve' pupil results"
card:
**What it is.** A news article from an established international broadcaster, published in September 2015, reporting on Study A, the international assessment report above. This is secondary reporting, not a study. Read it after Study A and compare the two.

**Headline.** Computers 'do not improve' pupil results, says [the organization].

**Opening paragraphs, verbatim.** "Investing heavily in school computers and classroom technology does not improve pupils' performance, says a global study from the [organization]." "The think tank says frequent use of computers in schools is more likely to be associated with lower results."

**What else the article says.** It quotes the organization's education director that school technology had raised "too many false hopes" and that "those students who use tablets and computers very often tend to do worse than those who use them moderately." A bulleted summary reports that moderate users, "such as once or twice a week," have "somewhat better learning outcomes" than rare users. The article notes the director's caveat that the findings "should not be used as an 'excuse' not to use technology," and gives space to an education technology association, a head teacher, and a technology company executive who disagree with the headline reading. It says the tests were "taken in more than 70 countries."

**Questions to ask.** The headline and first sentence state a result ("does not improve") that the underlying report describes as a correlation it "cannot" interpret causally. The nuance about moderate use appears, but after the categorical lead. The "more than 70 countries" figure describes the assessment as a whole; the key curves rest on 20 to 29 wealthy countries. Which of these differences matter for a school board member who reads only the headline?

**Who produced it and why.** A staff education correspondent at a publicly funded national broadcaster. The outlet does not sell technology. Its incentive is readership, and a categorical headline draws more of it than "hill-shaped association, causation unclear."
